chapter_theme: In the fifth part of the debate with the Buddha, Neelakesi mocks his former-birth gifts (the rain for worms, the body split open, the wife and children given away), argues that denying the soul refutes itself, and then answers his account of karma without a doer, the seed-and-sprout continuity and the lac-stained pomegranate seed, by pressing that nothing beyond the five aggregates carries a deed to its fruit.

cast.role: the demoness of the burning-ground temple who takes the Jain dharma and becomes its debater
the Buddha, whom Neelakesi debates in person in the புத்த வாதச் சருக்கம்

563.reading: Neelakesi asks the Buddha, whom she hails as the one famed for sending rain so that worms might live, to explain how gifts of great wealth made by farmers, merchants and others to the faultless are said to turn out differently, since faultless people are to be seen too.
563.nuance: The closing epithet turns a former-birth tale of compassion (rain sent for worms) into mockery; the sense of lines 1-3, whether the fruit of a gift is said to differ by its receiver, rests on a compressed construction.

564.reading: Neelakesi asks whether worship paid by those convinced that something is a god, and giving mixed with the wish to be rid of what is in one's hand, are not all faults when examined, addressing the Buddha as the noble one who split his own body to give to those who asked.
564.nuance: Line 3 (மெய்தல் ரேயின்) is damaged; reading it as 'if one examines truly' makes the verse a charge that the Buddha's body-gifts fall under faults his own side names.

claims.claim: worship offered from belief in a god and giving driven by desire are faults

565.reading: Neelakesi asks whether jewelled women are goods fit to be given as alms, and whether those who take charge of them once they are handed over can be shown not to be thieves, mocking the Buddha's greatness in giving to others out of compassion while his own children wailed.
565.nuance: The objection shifts ground from earlier attacks on the body-gifts: here the wrong is that persons are not the giver's property, so the gift turns the receiver into a thief. The word கருணையால் is used against the compassion it names.

claims.claim: wives and children are not goods that may be given away, and whoever takes them so is a thief

566.reading: Neelakesi says that the Buddha made the teaching that nothing endures his path, and that if after ruining everything in many ways he then offers a remedy he cannot keep to the truth he declared, hailing him as the one whose virtue stopped the murderous wrathful elephant.
566.nuance: The epithet in line 4 recalls the taming of a raging elephant; the argument that a remedy presupposes something lasting is a reading of the compressed lines 2-3.

claims.claim: nothing endures, and to teach this is the path
one who denies all endurance cannot consistently offer a remedy afterwards

567.reading: Neelakesi argues that if the Buddha holds there is no soul at all, then admitting even one faultless mark as soul destroys his thesis, and if he denies the soul only through a constructed fiction (பரிகற்பனை) he has by his own view conceded that it exists.
567.nuance: Line 3's ஏதிலார் சொல் may mean 'the word of strangers' or 'unrelated words'; either way the move is that a denial made by mere construction admits the thing denied.

claims.claim: there is no soul at all
to deny a thing only by a constructed designation is to concede that it exists

568.reading: Neelakesi asks the Buddha, who said the soul is nothing, who then he is that accepts being and non-being standing as they are as the path, and says that since the nine heads he spoke of before cannot hold by any means, he has today taken her Lord as the Lord.
568.nuance: The question நீ யாவனோ turns the no-self thesis on the speaker. What the nine (நவத்திறம்) are is not said in this verse.

claims.claim: one who denies the soul cannot say who it is that holds a view

569.reading: Neelakesi asks whether, if there is no knower who recollects, the Buddhist can explain knowing by any of seven ways: by likeness, by unlikeness, by construction, by 'nothing other than it', by the strength of deeds, by yoga, or by the moment of clear understanding.
569.nuance: The list is compressed and the reading of some items (புனைவு, யோகு) is tentative; the point is that recollection (மீட்டுணர்வு) needs one who knows across time.

claims.claim: without an enduring knower, recollection cannot be accounted for by likeness, karma, yoga or any other means

570.reading: Neelakesi appeals to the four ways of designating the soul that begin with the soul-in-name, says the Buddha's word changes if purity belongs to the soul in the first three, and asks whether by these he can deny the soul's existence.
570.nuance: நாம சீவன் முதலாய நான்மை looks like the Jain fourfold placing of a word (by name, by representation, by substance, by state); தாம சீவன் and வாம சீவன் in lines 3-4 are obscure and may be corrupt.

claims.claim: the soul is spoken of in four ways beginning with the soul in name, and these do not allow its existence to be denied

571.reading: Neelakesi says she has shattered the knower, truth, the five aggregates and everything else by showing that none of them stands, and bids the Buddha name anything left; the Buddha answers that he will subdue her by his own path, and bids her consider.
571.event: Neelakesi declares the Buddha's categories refuted and challenges him to name another; the Buddha says he will subdue her by his own path.

572.reading: Neelakesi says she will not accept a path without reason except from those who teach the wide wandering that has no beginning, the means that cuts off birth, and the fit between a deed and its fruit.
572.nuance: The verse sets her terms for the reply that follows: any account the Buddha gives must show how a deed's fruit reaches its doer. That ஒப்பு means the deed-fruit correspondence is a reading.

claims.claim: the round of births has no beginning
a path is acceptable only if it shows how birth is cut off and how a deed's fruit fits the deed

573.reading: The Buddha says that as sprout and branch appear in succession from a seed, he calls the continuity arising by potency a change, that release is not other than this, and bids Neelakesi take it as the truth.
573.nuance: Neelakesi answers the seed image in 579-583, where she argues the analogy carries nothing across for the aggregates. The account is given in a Jain work.

claims.claim: a person is a continuity (சந்தானம்) arising by potency, as sprout and branch from a seed
release is not other than the course of this continuity

574.reading: The Buddha says that the deed exists and its fruit exists, but there is not a millet-grain's worth of a doer, and that none of the aggregates stands for even a moment.
574.nuance: Neelakesi answers at once in 575 and again in 584. The thesis matches the Buddhist teacher's own words in Manimekalai 30 (the chain has no maker), so here the polemic attacks a view the school holds.

claims.claim: deeds and their fruits exist, but there is no doer
none of the aggregates lasts beyond a moment

575.reading: Neelakesi answers that the Buddha calls virtue a real thing and giving a real thing, yet says there is no one who knows, acts and enjoys, and that if the aggregates last only a moment even his own name quarrels with him.
575.nuance: The jab at his name is a reading of பிணங்குவது ஒக்கும் நின் பேர்: the 'awakened one' cannot be a knower if there is no knower.

claims.claim: there is no one who knows, acts and enjoys the fruit
merit and giving make no sense without one who knows, acts and enjoys

576.reading: The Buddha says an evil mind brings the suffering of burning and a mind of worth brings bliss hereafter, as when a pomegranate seed is steeped in lac its red is seen in the flower.
576.nuance: The lac-and-pomegranate image is the Buddhist answer to how a deed reaches its fruit without a lasting self; Neelakesi takes it apart in 579-585.

claims.claim: an evil mind leads to burning suffering and a worthy one to bliss, as lac on a pomegranate seed reddens its flower

577.reading: The Buddha goes on that the seed and the lac are each made of eight constituents, and that the red and the other marks appear in the flower's eye and colour, and so it is here.
577.nuance: எட்டின் இயன்ற reads as the Buddhist octad of matter; line 4 (காடம்டுவ) is damaged and the second half of the verse is hard to construe.

claims.claim: seed and lac are each made of eight material constituents

578.reading: The Buddha gives his parallel: two youths made of the five aggregates, one of wholesome and one of unwholesome deeds, so that from the good-minded one comes a god and from the one of cruel deeds a hell-dweller.
578.nuance: The terms குசல and அகுசல are the Buddhist words for wholesome and unwholesome action; Neelakesi answers the parallel in 579-580.

claims.claim: a being of five aggregates continues as a god or a hell-dweller according to wholesome or unwholesome deeds

579.reading: Neelakesi says the seed is only the eight and nothing else, and the five aggregates are likewise, so she asks how his example fits and bids him hear while she takes it up and rebukes it.

580.reading: Neelakesi argues that the lac is something added to the eightfold seed, but he shows no such further thing for the five aggregates, and tells the deluded Buddha to stop showing the pomegranate.
580.nuance: This is the same dilemma she put to Kundalakesi in 203: whatever carries the deed across is a further thing beyond the five, which is what the Jain calls a soul.

claims.claim: the lac analogy fails because the lac is a thing beyond the seed, and nothing beyond the five aggregates is admitted to carry a deed

581.reading: Neelakesi says that showing the colour in the flower does not fit, since a man's deed bears fruit in the god he becomes, and asks whether the Buddha has set aside that the act too perishes when the pomegranate dies.
581.nuance: Lines 2-4 are compressed (மாவின்கண் may be 'in the mango' or a place-word); the reading that the flower is the wrong place for the fruit of a deed is tentative.

582.reading: Neelakesi says that even if he shows a difference between seed and flower, he must speak of the infant and the old man, and that babbling like the mad he cannot join a deed to its fruit in any way.
582.nuance: The infant and the old man are one person at two times: Neelakesi moves the question from a plant's series to the life of one human, where the doer and the enjoyer should be the same.

claims.claim: on the Buddhist account a deed cannot be joined to its fruit

583.reading: Neelakesi asks: if the seed's form, faded with the lac, skips the sprout and settles in the flower, what would he say of Angulimala?
583.nuance: Angulimala, the killer who became the Buddha's disciple, is named without his story; how his case bears on the argument (whether his killings bore fruit) is not spelled out here.

584.reading: Neelakesi asks whether, if he says the lac comes to be like that by such a course, he will also say that one man toils at the deed while another, born a god, enjoys its fruit.
584.nuance: The objection is that without a lasting self the one who acts and the one who enjoys are two; line 2 (தப்படையான் உழப் பெய்வழி) is obscure and the reading rests on the sense of the whole.

claims.claim: without a lasting self the doer of a deed and the enjoyer of its fruit would be different persons

585.reading: Neelakesi argues that his flower example cannot carry a deed's sweet fruit from one birth to the next, so by his account there would be neither this birth nor the next.
585.nuance: Line 2 is damaged (a non-Tamil character stands for its first letter), and line 1 is hard to construe.

claims.claim: on the Buddhist account there would be neither this birth nor the next

586.reading: Neelakesi draws a consequence: if the fruit of many flowers is reckoned as eaten because they were seen as its cause, then deer flesh and fish meat in the begging bowl could pass for bees' food.
586.nuance: The construction is obscure; that the absurd consequence aims at the Buddhist monk's eating of meat (மண்டை, the bowl) is a reading.

links.note: The Buddha of the Neelakesi offers seed, sprout and branch as a continuity in which release lies; the Manimekalai's teacher uses seed, sprout and stalk as the example of the continuity name, one word for a series.
links.teaches: The Buddhist epic uses the seed series as a rule of naming, while the Jain epic puts it in the Buddha's mouth as an account of what passes on to release, which is the stronger claim its heroine can then attack.

links.note: The Buddha here says deed and fruit exist but no doer; Manimekalai 30's teacher says the chain has no maker, no I and no mine, and is itself deed and fruit.
links.teaches: Set against the Buddhist epic's own teaching, the Jain poem's Buddhist thesis turns out to be stated fairly, so Neelakesi's reply in 575 attacks a view the school holds, not a straw figure.

links.note: The Buddha denies any doer behind the deed; the quatrain says an old deed seeks out the very one who did it, as a calf finds its mother among many cows.
links.teaches: The quatrain's comfort that a deed finds its own doer depends on there being a doer who lasts, which is exactly what the Buddha's thesis denies, so the proverb takes a side in the Jain-Buddhist debate.

gains.a: the Buddha's thesis gains an everyday image of the persisting owner it rejects, showing what ordinary moral talk would lose under it
gains.b: the quatrain gains an opponent who makes explicit that its calf image assumes a lasting self

links.note: In 203 Neelakesi told Kundalakesi that a power passing between moments is either a sixth thing beyond the five aggregates or total destruction; here she tells the Buddha the lac is a further thing, and the aggregates have none.
links.teaches: The same dilemma defeats the disciple's power and the teacher's lac, which shows Neelakesi's case is one argument: every Buddhist carrier of karma is either a soul under another name or nothing.

links.note: Kundalakesi gave the Buddha's gifts of wife and child as proof of his compassion; Neelakesi tells the Buddha that those who take such gifts cannot be shown not to be thieves.
links.teaches: The gift offered as proof of compassion is answered not only as the giver's folly, as in 207, but as a wrong done through the receiver, since a wife and children were never the giver's to give.

links.note: The couplet defines a gift by its receiver: what goes to those who have nothing. Neelakesi tests a gift by what is given: persons handed over as alms make their taker a thief.
links.teaches: A gift can satisfy the couplet's test of the receiver's want and still fail, because the thing given must be the giver's own, which the couplet takes for granted.

gains.a: Neelakesi's objection gains a householder's definition of giving that does not mention property, showing her test adds a condition
gains.b: the couplet gains a limit it leaves unstated: one may give only what is one's own, and persons are not

new_concepts.gloss: the five aggregates (form, feeling, perception, formation, consciousness) that are spoken of as a person
new_concepts.label_source: the verse's own word: ஐங்கந்தம் (571), கந்தம் (574, 575)

new_concepts.gloss: the Buddha: the awakened teacher of dharma, his coming in a dark age, and the worship of his seat and footprints
formal debate between schools before a king and assembly, with stakes for the loser; distinct from vaadham, the alchemy of the Siddhars
new_concepts.label_source: the sarukkam title names it (புத்த வாதச் சருக்கம்); the id follows earlier chapters, since vaadham is taken

source_issues: 564 line 3: மெய்தல் ரேயின் is damaged; perhaps மெய் தேரின்.
570 lines 3-4: தாம சீவன் and வாம சீவன் are obscure and may be corrupt.
577 line 4: காடம்டுவ is not a word; the line is corrupt.
581 lines 2-4 and 584 line 2 (தப்படையான்) are hard to construe and may be corrupt.
585 line 2: the first letter is the non-Tamil character ¦ (U+00A6), an encoding error; perhaps செம்மை.
563 line 3 and others: the old encoding • for ஃ was repaired by the build.
